name: LCROSS Centaur
intro: This was the empty Centaur upper stage of the rocket that launched LCROSS and the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. Instead of drifting in space, it was aimed at Cabeus, a crater near the south pole whose floor never sees sunlight. Its crash threw up a plume that contained water.
whyLeft: It was used up after launch, so NASA turned the empty rocket stage into a giant hammer to dig into the dark crater.
repurpose: The ice it uncovered is the real treasure: future crews may turn ice like this into drinking water, air and rocket fuel.
funFact: The Centaur weighed more than 2 tonnes and hit at about 2.5 km per second, roughly 9,000 km per hour.

hotspots.title: Dark crater floor
hotspots.text: The Centaur hit here, in the floor of Cabeus, a crater 98 km wide that sunlight never reaches. It came in steeply, at about 75 degrees, and dug a new crater in the frozen soil.

hotspots.title: Impact flash
hotspots.text: The LCROSS shepherding spacecraft, following behind, saw a small bright flash in the darkness when the Centaur hit. That flash was the empty rocket stage turning into heat and light.

photo.alt: An infrared picture with a small white spot inside a dark crater shadow
photo.caption: The impact flash (the small white spot) seen by LCROSS’s mid-infrared camera.
photo.licenseEvidence: Wikimedia Commons file page: licence “Public domain” (PD-USGov-NASA: work of NASA, not copyrighted in the US); credited NASA/LCROSS, published on NASA’s Astronomy Picture of the Day

hotspots.title: Plume of ice
hotspots.text: The crash blasted dust and ice high into the sunlight. Instruments counted about 155 kg of water vapour and ice in the cloud: proof that the Moon’s coldest craters hide frozen water.

source.label: Colaprete et al. (NASA Ames), Science 2010: water in the LCROSS plume

hotspots.title: Hot spot
hotspots.text: Ninety seconds after the crash, the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter flew over and measured a hot spot in one of the coldest places in the Solar System.

photo.alt: Two thermal maps of the impact site, before and after, the second with a warm spot
photo.caption: Heat maps of the impact site from LRO’s Diviner instrument: two hours before the crash, and 90 seconds after.
photo.licenseEvidence: Wikimedia Commons file page: licence “Public domain” (PD-USGov-NASA: work of NASA, not copyrighted in the US); from nasa.gov LCROSS mission pages, credit NASA/GSFC/UCLA

hotspots.title: Rocket remains
hotspots.text: Scout, there is nothing left to fix: the Centaur was an empty fuel tank with an engine, and the impact shattered it. Its pieces lie buried somewhere in the frozen, pitch-black soil.
